title: Seahawks Pass on Joe Mixon After Physical: No Practice Squad Deal, NBC Sports Reports
body:
Seattle’s pursuit of veteran running back Joe Mixon hit an unexpected snag on Monday, as the Seahawks announced they will not add the former Cincinnati Bengals star to their practice squad following a routine physical. The decision leaves Mixon, who has been out of the league since a torn ACL ended his 2023 season, without a team and further delays any hopes of a swift return to the NFL.

The Seahawks had invited Mixon to a workout earlier this week, a move that sparked speculation that Seattle might use the veteran as a low‑cost depth option should injuries strike the backfield. Head coach Mike Macdonald confirmed that the organization began the standard signing process after the workout, but the subsequent medical evaluation revealed concerns that could not be cleared. “We went through the proper protocol, and after the physical we decided not to move forward,” Macdonald said in a brief press conference. The exact nature of the medical issue was not disclosed, but insiders suggest lingering instability in the knee that required additional imaging.

Mixon’s situation is emblematic of the broader challenges faced by running backs trying to re‑enter the league after serious injuries. The position has become increasingly volatile, with teams often favoring younger, cheaper talent over veterans with injury histories. In 2023, the average career length for a running back hovered around 2.7 years, and a major injury like an ACL tear can drastically shorten that window. For Mixon, who posted 1,200 rushing yards and 10 touchdowns in 2022, the setback is particularly painful, as he entered free agency with a reputation as a reliable, dual‑threat back capable of contributing both on the ground and in the passing game.

Seattle’s backfield situation remains fluid. The Seahawks currently rely on rookie running back Kenneth Walker III, who has shown flashes of explosiveness but also endured a mid‑season injury that limited his workload. Veteran Alexander Matthews, now in his 13th season, provides a veteran presence but is clearly on the roster’s periphery. The team’s front office has been exploring multiple avenues to bolster depth, including a potential trade for a seasoned backup or signing a free‑agent special‑teams contributor. The Mixon episode underscores the difficulty of finding a seasoned, cost‑effective option that can pass the league’s rigorous medical standards.

From a strategic standpoint, the Seahawks’ decision may also reflect a broader shift in how teams assess risk versus reward in the modern NFL. While a player of Mixon’s caliber could theoretically provide a one‑dimensional boost in short‑yardage scenarios, the financial and roster implications of carrying an injured player on the practice squad—especially under the current salary‑cap constraints—may outweigh the upside. Moreover, the league’s evolving practice‑squad rules, which now allow for a limited number of veterans, have not eliminated the necessity of thorough medical vetting, a process that appears to have halted Mixon’s Seattle opportunity.

Looking ahead, Mixon’s path back to the league will likely involve a combination of continued rehabilitation and targeted outreach to teams with immediate needs at running back. The NFL offseason will see a flurry of workouts and tryouts, and a fully healed Mixon could still attract interest, particularly from clubs dealing with depth concerns or those willing to gamble on a proven talent at a reduced cost. For Seattle, the focus will shift to developing Walker and evaluating other low‑risk options that can provide stability without compromising the roster’s health. As the league’s calendar moves toward free‑agency day, both Mixon and the Seahawks will be watching closely for any opening that aligns health, opportunity, and strategic fit.
